oneSentence: A document approved through a recognised international standards process that sets common requirements, guidance or methods for repeated use.
plainExplanation:
An international standard is a shared set of rules, requirements or test methods published by a standards body such as ISO or IEC. The input is usually a practical problem: for example, different systems cannot exchange data, safety checks vary, or organisations need a common way to manage risk.

Experts from different countries and sectors draft and negotiate the text. They compare needs, define terms, choose requirements and sometimes add ways to test whether those requirements are being met. The process aims for broad agreement, but the exact procedure depends on the standards body.

The output is a document that others can use voluntarily, or that governments, contracts or regulators may later refer to. That document might describe how to format data, how to measure performance, or how an organisation should run a management system.

This is often confused with regulation, but they are not the same. A regulation is a legal rule made by a public authority. A standard is usually not law by itself, though a law or procurement rule can incorporate it. It is also different from interoperability: interoperability is the ability of systems to work together, while a standard is one tool that can help achieve that.

everydayAnalogy.title: Two offices rewriting the same update
everydayAnalogy.story: A team in Nairobi and a team in Bangkok both need to send a short situation update to a regional office. At first, each office writes in its own style, so one message starts with dates, another with locations, and key facts appear in different places. Then the regional office gives everyone the same template: first location, then date, then incident summary, then actions needed. The updates still use different words, but they arrive in a format that others can read quickly and compare more easily.

mapping.analogyElement: offices in different places using one format
mapping.aiElement: different organisations or countries following common requirements
users, buyers or regulators benefiting from consistency

mapping.analogyElement: different wording within the same structure
mapping.aiElement: local implementation while following common rules

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A standard is more than a simple template. It can include detailed definitions, test methods, measurement criteria and governance requirements, not just a layout. Also, real international standards are developed through formal processes in recognised standards bodies, not handed down by one office.

visual.title: How an international standard turns a shared problem into a common reference
visual.learningObjective: After viewing, a reader should be able to explain what goes into an international standard, how it is developed, and what comes out for users.
visual.description: Show a left-to-right flow with four boxes connected by arrows. Read from problem to drafting to publication to use. Each box contains a short label and one sentence. Add a small note under the last box showing that use may be voluntary or referenced by law, contracts or procurement.

steps.label: 1. Shared problem
steps.explanation: Different products, services or organisations do similar things in incompatible or inconsistent ways.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with three small mismatched icons inside, such as data tables with different column orders or plugs with different shapes.

steps.label: 2. Drafting and negotiation
steps.explanation: Experts from multiple countries and sectors define terms, requirements and sometimes test methods through a formal standards process.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with several person icons around a document, with speech lines converging into one text page.

steps.label: 3. Published standard
steps.explanation: The result is a document that states common requirements, methods or management practices.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box with a labelled document icon and three bullet lines titled terms, requirements, tests.

steps.label: 4. Adoption and reference
steps.explanation: Organisations may use the document directly, and governments or buyers may cite it in rules, contracts or procurement.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box feeding into three smaller icons: organisation, contract, regulation, each receiving the same document.

visual.interaction: Hover or tap each box to reveal a short example, such as data format, safety test, or management system requirement.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow. Step 1 shows a shared problem: similar systems or organisations work in different ways, causing inconsistency or incompatibility. Step 2 shows experts from different countries and sectors drafting and negotiating a text through a formal process. Step 3 shows the published result: a standard containing common terms, requirements or test methods. Step 4 shows how others use it: organisations may adopt it voluntarily, and public authorities or buyers may also reference it in laws, contracts or procurement. The main point is that a standard converts a common coordination problem into a common reference document.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static four-box flow appears with arrows from left to right: shared problem, drafting and negotiation, published standard, adoption and reference. Example notes appear below each box without animation.

workedExample.scenario: Three health ministries and two software suppliers want AI-assisted chest X-ray systems to record findings in a comparable way across borders.
workedExample.input: Current outputs vary: one system writes 'possible pneumonia', another writes 'lung infection likely', and confidence scores use different scales from 0-1, 0-100 and low-medium-high.
process: A standards group defines shared terms for key findings and a common format for confidence reporting.
It sets test methods so suppliers can show whether their systems produce outputs in the required structure.
The standard is published, and a regional procurement notice asks vendors to comply with it.
Two suppliers update their software so result files use the same fields and score scale.
workedExample.result: Hospitals can compare results more easily, procurement teams can write clearer requirements, and software from different suppliers is more likely to work with the same reporting workflow.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A UN team preparing guidance on AI procurement for multilingual document processing compares whether suppliers follow recognised international standards for management systems, quality and interoperability-related specifications.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: This helps staff ask more precise questions, compare vendors on a common basis and avoid relying only on marketing claims.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Do not upload confidential internal documents, personal data or protection-sensitive field material into an unapproved public AI service to test whether a product meets a standard; use approved review processes and human oversight.

whyItMatters: For non-specialists, international standards matter because they often shape what counts as acceptable, safe, compatible or auditable in practice. They can lower costs, make procurement clearer, improve cross-border compatibility and give regulators or organisations a ready-made technical reference. But they are not automatically neutral or perfect. Who participated, whose needs were prioritised, and whether smaller or lower-resource actors could contribute all affect the result. If you confuse a standard with a law, you may overestimate its legal force. If you ignore standards completely, you may miss an important part of how AI systems are governed in everyday operations.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An international standard is automatically a binding global law.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Usually it is not law by itself. Standards are commonly voluntary documents published by recognised bodies. They can become influential or effectively mandatory if a regulator, contract, buyer or certification scheme refers to them, but that legal effect comes from the referencing instrument, not from the standard alone.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If something follows a standard, it must be safe or high quality in every respect.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A standard covers the topics inside its scope, not everything that matters. A product may conform to one standard and still perform poorly on issues the document does not address, such as local language quality, human rights impacts, accessibility or context-specific risks.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Standards and interoperability mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Interoperability is an outcome: systems can work together. A standard is a tool that may support that outcome by defining common formats, interfaces or terms. Some standards do not concern interoperability at all, and some systems can interoperate through bilateral design choices without using a formal international standard.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A common reference that helps organisations build, test or manage things consistently.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: An international standard is a document approved through a recognised international standards process. It specifies agreed requirements, guidance, characteristics, terminology, interfaces, measurement methods, test procedures or management system practices for common and repeated use. In AI, standards may address data formats, documentation, risk management, quality management, testing or governance controls. Normative instrument is a broader category of formally adopted texts. Standards follow a standards development process and commonly provide requirements, guidance or methods. They may support interoperability, but interoperability is the result of systems working together. Standards are generally voluntary, although regulation, procurement, contracts or certification arrangements may require conformity.

keyTakeaway: A standard gives many actors one shared reference point, but it is not the same thing as a law or a guarantee of good outcomes.

quickCheck.question: Which statement best describes an international standard?
options: A document from a recognised standards body that sets common requirements or methods and may later be referenced by laws or contracts.
A binding rule adopted automatically by all countries once experts agree on technical language.
Any best-practice guide published by a company for its own customers.
A guarantee that any AI system using it will be safe and interoperable in all contexts.
quickCheck.explanation: An international standard comes through a recognised international standards process and sets common requirements, guidance or methods. A regulation is a binding rule from a public authority. Normative instrument is broader, while interoperability is an outcome that a standard may support.

contested: The basic idea is widely accepted, but details vary across standards bodies and legal systems, especially around how much consensus is required and how standards interact with regulation, procurement and certification.

issues.problem: The definition only requires a recognised standards body. A national or regional standards body can also be recognised, so this does not distinguish an international standard.
issues.fix: A document approved through a recognised international standards process that sets common requirements, guidance or methods for repeated use.

issues.problem: The explanation distinguishes regulation and interoperability but not normative instrument. It therefore leaves the standard blurred with the broader category of formally adopted texts that set principles, expectations or guidance.
issues.fix: State that normative instrument is the broader category, while an international standard is approved through a recognised international standards process and commonly provides requirements, guidance or methods for repeated use.

issues.problem: Calling a standard a "rulebook" blurs it with regulation and normative instruments. Standards may provide guidance or methods rather than rules.
issues.fix: A common reference that helps organisations build, test or manage things consistently.

issues.problem: The definition again requires only a recognised standards development body, which could be national. It also says the document is for use "across jurisdictions and sectors", although an international standard can be limited to one sector.
issues.fix: Specify a recognised international standards process and common or repeated use. Remove the claim that every international standard operates across sectors, and distinguish standards from normative instruments and interoperability.

issues.problem: The example says only that "a standards group" defines the terms. That could produce a private consortium specification rather than an international standard. The example never establishes a recognised international standards process.
issues.fix: A recognised international standards body defines shared terms and a common confidence format.

issues.problem: The visual refers only to a formal standards process. It does not show the feature that makes the output international rather than national, regional or private.
issues.fix: Replace "formal standards process" with "recognised international standards process" in both places.

issues.problem: The marked option says only "a recognised standards body". This can include a national body, so the option is not an adequate definition of an international standard.
issues.fix: A document approved through a recognised international standards process that sets common requirements, guidance or methods.

issues.problem: All three distractors announce their falsity through absolutes such as "automatically", "all countries", "any", "guarantee" and "all contexts". A reader can answer without distinguishing international standard from regulation, normative instrument or interoperability.
issues.fix: Use these distractors: "A binding technical rule adopted by a public authority for organisations to follow."; "Shared principles adopted outside a standards development process."; "The ability of systems to exchange information and use it correctly."
